Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from what I've gathered. I'll note that I was limited to 4 fetches and 5 searches, but what I obtained is substantial.

# Romans 4 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Paul uses Abraham (and David) as his crowning Old Testament witnesses that justification has always been by faith, not works. The chapter falls into four movements: (1) Abraham was justified by faith, not works (vv.1–8); (2) this was before circumcision, so Gentiles share the blessing (vv.9–12); (3) the promise was through faith-righteousness, not law (vv.13–17); (4) the nature of Abraham's faith and its application to Christians (vv.18–25). — Ellicott summarises: "The true seed of Abraham are those who follow his example of faith." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

---

## v. 1 – "What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather, has found?"

- **Paul's rhetorical strategy.** Paul uses a diatribe style (rhetorical questions with imaginary interlocutors) common in ancient philosophical schools. "What then shall we say?" marks the transition and anticipates Jewish objections to his doctrine of justification by faith alone. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_41-3)

- **Why Abraham?** Abraham was the most esteemed figure among Jews — greater even than Moses in some respects, being called "the Friend" of God (2 Chron 20:7; Isa 41:8). If even Abraham was justified by faith and not works, then the case is closed for everyone else. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **"According to the flesh."** Ellicott notes the phrase belongs with "our father" — meaning "our father by natural descent" (as in Rom 1:3). The alternative reading (connecting it with "has found") would ask what Abraham obtained by natural human effort, which fits Paul's argument about works. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Rabbinic background.** Jewish teachers of Paul's day taught that Abraham was justified by works — some even said he kept the whole Law before it was given, by intuition or anticipation. Ancient rabbinic sources say: "We find that Abraham our father had performed the whole Law before it was given." Paul is directly countering this prevailing view. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 2 – "If Abraham was indeed justified by works, he had something to boast about, but not before God."

- **The logic.** If Abraham earned justification by works, he would have grounds for boasting — but only before men, never before God. Ellicott calls this Paul's "rapid and eager dialectic": whatever boasting might exist before other people, "there is no boasting before God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **MacArthur's syllogism.** John MacArthur (Baptist) outlines Paul's reasoning as a hypothetical syllogism: Major premise — if a man could be justified by works, he has ground for boasting. Minor premise — Abraham was justified by works. Conclusion — Abraham has something to boast about. The major premise is true, but Paul goes on to show the minor premise is false; therefore the conclusion fails. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_41-3)

- **Guzik adds:** Boasting is "nothing before God" because even if works could justify, every person still falls short of God's glory (Rom 3:23). Before God, every pretence is stripped away. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 3 – "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." (Gen 15:6)

- **The key proof-text.** Paul quotes Genesis 15:6, the foundational text for justification by faith. The Old Testament does not say Abraham was declared righteous because of his works; it says he believed and it was "credited" (logizomai) to him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **"Credited" (logizomai).** Wuest explains this word was used in secular documents for "put down to one's account, let my revenues be placed on deposit." God deposited righteousness into Abraham's account — Abraham possessed it as one possesses money in a bank. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Imputation, not infusion.** Ellicott is emphatic: "The sense of imputation is not to be got rid of. It is distinctly a forensic act. The righteousness attributed to Abraham is not an actual righteousness, but something else that is considered and treated as if it were equivalent." God acts as judge, not as one infusing a quality into the soul. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Gill: what is the "it" credited?** John Gill (Baptist, older) argues at length that the "it" credited is not the grace of faith itself (faith is not righteousness, nor is it accounted as such), but rather "the promised seed, the Messiah, and his righteousness, which Abraham, by faith, looked unto, and believed in." Faith is distinguished from righteousness and is the instrument by which a person lays hold of Christ's righteousness. This same "it" is imputed to all believers (v.24). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/4.htm)

- **Guzik:** "Paul does not say that Abraham was made righteous in all of his doings, but God accounted Abraham as righteous. Our justification is not God making us perfectly righteous, but counting us as perfectly righteous." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Calvin (quoted by Guzik):** "Moses [in Genesis] does not, indeed, tell us what men thought of him [Abraham], but how he was accounted before the tribunal of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 4 – "Now the wages of the worker are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation."

- **Grace vs. works.** Paul draws a sharp antithesis: in a works-based system, reward is not a gift (charis, grace) but a debt (opheilēma) that the employer owes. Grace and merit are opposite principles. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Ellicott:** "The relation between what he receives and what he does is that of wages for work done. He can claim it, if need be, in a court of law. There is in it no element of grace, or favour, or concession." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik):** "Grace and faith are congruous, and will draw together in the same chariot, but grace and merit are contrary the one to the other and pull opposite ways, and therefore God has not chosen to yoke them together." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 5 – "To the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the wicked, his faith is credited as righteousness."

- **God justifies the ungodly.** This is the radical heart of the gospel. Paul uses the strongest possible word — "the ungodly" (asebēs, the impious). God does not wait for people to become godly before justifying them. Ellicott: "It is characteristic of the Apostle not to flinch from the boldest expression." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **"Does not work" — not laziness.** Murray (Reformed, quoted by Guzik) clarifies: "The antithesis is not simply between the worker and the non-worker but between the worker and the person who does not work but believes." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Denney (quoted by Guzik):** "The paradoxical phrase, Him that justifieth the ungodly, does not suggest that justification is a fiction, whether legal or of any other sort, but that it is a miracle." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Faith as instrument, not ground.** Ligonier (Reformed): "Faith alone is the instrument that we exercise to lay hold of the ground upon which the Lord's verdict of righteousness is pronounced; faith is not the basis or ground upon which God makes His declaration." The Greek preposition eis is better translated "unto" righteousness, not "as" righteousness — faith is counted with respect to righteousness, not as equivalent to it. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/counting-faith-righteousness)

- **Sproul (Reformed):** "That does not mean that your faith is the righteousness that is the grounds for your salvation. No, faith only lays hold of Christ. It is the instrument by which you are linked to Jesus. Only Christ's righteousness is the grounds of your justification." (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/abraham-justified-faith)

---

## vv. 6–8 – David: "Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven... Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him."

- **David as second witness.** Paul calls David to the stand alongside Abraham. David knew what it was to be a guilty sinner (adultery, murder). If judged on works alone, God must condemn him — yet David experienced the blessedness of imputed righteousness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Ellicott:** David's evidence shows that justification "implies, not the absence of sin, but its forgiveness; not its real obliteration, but the forbearance of God to impute it. It is an amnesty, not an acquittal." Sins are "not abolished, but forgiven; not annihilated, but covered up, removed from sight, hidden by the absolving grace of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Imputation language.** Guzik notes Matthew Poole's observation: "Our adversaries the papists oppose the imputation of Christ's righteousness to us; they cavil at the very word… and yet the apostle useth the word ten times in this chapter." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Lenski (Lutheran, quoted by Guzik):** "No sinner, and try he ever so hard, can possibly carry his own sins away and come back cleansed of guilt… every sin and its guilt cling to the sinner as close as does his own shadow, cling to all eternity unless God carries them away." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 9 – "Is this blessing only on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised?"

- The question follows naturally: if blessedness comes through forgiveness and imputed righteousness, is it restricted to Jews (the circumcised)? Paul's answer: no, because Abraham was declared righteous before he was circumcised. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

---

## v. 10 – "Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before."

- **Chronology is decisive.** Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15:6. Circumcision was not instituted until Genesis 17 — at least 14 years later (Abraham was 99). Therefore righteousness cannot depend on circumcision. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 11 – "He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised."

- **Sign and seal.** Ellicott: "Circumcision is so far from superseding faith that it was only the sign or seal of it. It ratified a state of things already existing when it was instituted." Circumcision was not the cause or condition of Israel's privileges but the sign and ratification. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Father of uncircumcised believers.** Abraham is father of all who believe, whether circumcised or not. The vital link to Abraham is faith, not the ritual. Guzik: "It must have been a shock for the Jewish readers of this letter to see that Paul called Abraham the father of uncircumcised people!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Gentile converts and "our father."** Ancient Jews did not allow circumcised Gentile converts to call Abraham "our father" in the synagogue — only natural-born Jews could. Paul demolishes that distinction: through faith, all believers can say "our father Abraham." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 12 – "Father of the circumcised who not only are circumcised, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had."

- Mere physical circumcision without faith does not make one a true child of Abraham. Ellicott: "Of the two things, faith itself, and circumcision the sign of faith, the first only was essential, and the second was useless without it." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

---

## v. 13 – "The promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not given through the law, but through the righteousness that comes by faith."

- **"Heir of the world."** This promise was explained by the Jews as referring to the universal sovereignty of the Messiah. Ellicott says three stages are indicated: (1) faith, (2) imputed righteousness, (3) access to the Messianic kingdom. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Promise pre-dates the Law.** All God's dealings with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob occurred before the Mosaic Law was given. Therefore the promise cannot be based on law-keeping. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Newell (quoted by Guzik):** "Faith is the ground of God's blessing. Abraham was a blessed man, indeed, but he became heir of the world on another principle entirely – simple faith." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 14 – "For if those who live by the law are heirs, faith is useless and the promise is worthless."

- Ellicott: If law-keepers are the heirs, faith is "emptied of its meaning, becomes an empty name, and the promise is rendered nugatory. There is nothing left for either to do." Faith and law cannot co-exist as principles of inheritance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

---

## v. 15 – "Because the law brings wrath. And where there is no law, there is no transgression."

- **Law's true function.** Ellicott: "The proper effect of law is punishment; for law only exposes sin." The law reveals offences and calls down punishment on them — it cannot bring the inheritance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **"Where there is no law there is no transgression."** Guzik explains that "transgression" (parabasis) specifically means overstepping a clearly defined line. Where no line is drawn, there is no actual transgression — though there is still sin in the broader sense of broken trust with God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 16 – "Therefore, the promise comes by faith, so that it may rest on grace and may be guaranteed to all Abraham's offspring..."

- **Faith and grace are correlative.** Ellicott: "Faith on man's part is correlative with grace on the part of God, and salvation being thus dependent upon grace is as wide and universal as grace itself. It knows no restriction of law." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **The promise is "guaranteed" (sure).** If law were the basis, salvation would be unsure because no one keeps the law perfectly. Grace makes the promise certain because it depends on God, not on human performance. Poole (quoted by Guzik): if the promise "were of the law, it would be unsure and uncertain, because of man's weakness, who is not able to perform it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **"The father of us all"** — Abraham is father of both believing Jews ("those who are of the law") and believing Gentiles ("those who are of the faith of Abraham"). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 17 – "I have made you a father of many nations... the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist."

- **"Before him whom he believed"** — Ellicott translates "in the presence of" God. Abraham stands confronting the Almighty as he did when the promise was first given. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **God who gives life to the dead.** This refers first to the quickening of Sarah's dead womb and Abraham's aged body, but with "an undercurrent of reference to the calling of the Gentiles" (Ellicott). Guzik adds: if God could call the dead womb of Sarah to life, He can call those dead in trespasses and sins (Eph 2:1) to new life. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **"Calls into being what does not yet exist."** Guzik quotes Smith: "I'm greatly comforted when God speaks about me as righteous, justified, glorified, holy, pure, and saintly. God can talk about such things before they exist, because He knows they will exist." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 18 – "Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed..."

- **"Against hope" = beyond human hope.** Ellicott translates: "grounded his faith upon hope — that internal subjective hope that was strong within him, though there were no objective grounds for hoping." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Faith and action.** Guzik stresses that Abraham's faith was not passive: "Abraham and Sarah had marital relations and trusted God for a miraculous result. This shows us that faith does not mean doing nothing, but doing everything with trust and reliance on God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

- **Trapp (quoted by Guzik):** "Sense corrects imagination, reason corrects sense, but faith corrects both. It will not be, saith sense; it cannot be, saith reason; it both can and will be, saith faith, for I have a promise for it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 19 – "Without weakening in his faith, he acknowledged the decrepitness of his body... and the lifelessness of Sarah's womb."

- **Textual issue.** Ellicott notes that the best manuscripts omit the negative ("not"), making it read: "Who, because he was not weak in faith, considered indeed — took full account of — the natural impediments to the fulfilment of the promise, and yet did not doubt." Guzik also notes this textual uncertainty. In either reading, Abraham faced the facts squarely but trusted God anyway. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 20 – "He did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God."

- **Giving glory to God.** Ellicott explains this does not necessarily mean verbal praise; it may refer to "the frank recognition of God's omnipotence involved in Abraham's faith" — faith itself glorifies God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Strengthened in faith.** Guzik notes the double sense: Abraham was strengthened in his faith, and he was also strengthened by his faith. Spurgeon (quoted) pleads: "Dear brother, little faith will save thee if it be true faith, but there are many reasons why you should seek an increase of it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 21 – "Being fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised."

- **Full persuasion (plērophoria).** Abraham's faith rose to full assurance, built not on circumstances but on the character and power of the promising God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 22 – "This is why 'it was credited to him as righteousness.'"

- This verse sums up Paul's entire argument from vv.1–21: Abraham's faith — a trusting, fully-persuaded, God-glorifying faith — was the occasion for God crediting righteousness to his account. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_422-25)

---

## vv. 23–24 – "The words 'it was credited to him' were written not only for Abraham, but also for us, to whom righteousness will be credited..."

- **Genesis 15:6 was written for us.** Paul insists that the Old Testament record was not merely historical but permanently designed for the benefit of all believers (cf. Rom 15:4). "This happened two thousand years before Paul, but Paul says God did not write those words for Abraham alone. For whom were they written then? For us, today." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_422-25)

- **Faith's object: "Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead."** Ellicott notes the association of ideas: the birth of Isaac resembles the resurrection of Christ in that both involved the exercise of Omnipotence — the same Omnipotence Abraham believed in, and we are to believe in. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Guzik:** "Paul's confidence is glorious: It shall be imputed to us who believe; this wasn't just for Abraham, but for us also." This is not a special arrangement for Abraham alone; every believer enters the same relationship with God through the same kind of faith. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

## v. 25 – "He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification."

- **"Delivered over" (paredothē).** Ellicott says this means delivered to death, as in Isaiah 53:12 (LXX). The death of Christ deals with our offences. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Death and resurrection — distinct roles.** Ellicott is careful: "The death of Christ is the proper cause of justification, or means of atonement… the resurrection of Christ is only the mediate or secondary cause of it. The atoning efficacy lay in His death, but the proof of that efficacy — the proof that it was really the Messiah who died — was to be seen in the Resurrection." He cites 1 Cor 15:17: "If Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins" — meaning the resurrection is the guarantee that the atoning death was effective. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

- **Guzik emphasises both:** The resurrection "demonstrates God the Father's perfect satisfaction with the Son's work on the cross. It proves that what Jesus did on the cross was in fact a perfect sacrifice made by One who remained perfect, even though bearing the sin of the world." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

---

# Traditions Compared (from what the sources yielded)

## Reformed / Presbyterian (Ligonier / R.C. Sproul)

- The central emphasis is on **forensic, legal imputation** of Christ's righteousness — an "alien righteousness" (Luther's phrase, *iustitia aliena*), outside of us (*extra nos*). Sproul: "The righteousness by which you are justified is the righteousness that Christ manifested in His life of perfect obedience." (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/abraham-justified-faith)
- Faith is strictly the **instrument**, never the ground, of justification. "If you add one ounce of your own righteousness as your confidence in your justification, you are repudiating the gospel." (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/abraham-justified-faith)
- The Reformed position explicitly contrasts with the Roman Catholic view of **infused righteousness** (righteousness poured into the soul at baptism, completed by penance and good works). Sproul: "If I have to wait until I am inherently righteous, I am a dead man." (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/abraham-justified-faith)
- *Simul iustus et peccator* — simultaneously righteous and sinner — is a hallmark Reformed/Lutheran emphasis drawn from this chapter. (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/abraham-justified-faith)

## Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

- Guzik affirms the traditional Protestant reading (imputation, faith alone) but emphasises **practical faith that acts**. He stresses that Abraham's faith "wasn't passive waiting but active obedience: he had marital relations with Sarah and trusted God for the miraculous result." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)
- There is strong emphasis on **application**: "We should examine whether we're trying to earn God's favor through our performance, or whether we're resting in the grace He freely gives." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)
- Guzik also stresses that the word "accounted" means God credits righteousness "like money deposited in a bank — we're counted righteous, not made righteous in all our doings." This is consistent with the Reformed forensic view. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-4/)

## Older Anglican / Broad Evangelical (Ellicott)

- Ellicott (1878) is careful, nuanced, and scholarly. He affirms forensic imputation: "The righteousness attributed to Abraham is not an actual righteousness, but something else that is considered and treated as if it were equivalent." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)
- He describes justification as "an amnesty, not an acquittal" — sins are forgiven and covered, not obliterated.
- He is careful about the death-resurrection distinction: the death atones; the resurrection proves and guarantees the atonement's efficacy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/romans-4.html)

## Baptist (John Gill, from available snippets)

- Gill (older Particular Baptist) argues vigorously that the "it" imputed is **not faith itself but Christ's righteousness**. Faith is distinguished from righteousness; it is the receiving instrument. "It remains then that it was the promised seed, the Messiah, and his righteousness, which Abraham, by faith, looked unto, and believed in, that was made unto him righteousness by imputation." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/4.htm)

---

## What Could Not Be Included (due to search/fetch limits)

- **Lutheran** distinctives (1517.org, LCMS) — would likely emphasise the *simul iustus et peccator* and the "great exchange" reading of vv.4–5
- **Methodist/Wesleyan** (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu) — would likely emphasise faith working through love and the "faith alone but not a faith that is alone" reading
- **Catholic** (newadvent.org, catholic.com) — would likely emphasise the Council of Trent's teaching that justification involves infusion of sanctifying grace, not mere imputation, and that faith must be accompanied by hope and charity
- **Orthodox** (oca.org) — would likely emphasise *theosis* (deification) and a less forensic, more transformational view of righteousness
- **Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) — would likely address the New Perspective on Paul, differences between "works of law" (boundary markers) vs. "good works," and the social function of Romans 4 in the Gentile mission
- **Hyper-grace / Word of Faith** — debates around v.5 ("justifies the ungodly") and whether ongoing repentance is required
